content: Acute spinal cord injury is a severe and life-altering condition that predominantly affects young individuals, particularly males. The administration of steroids in the early hours following such an injury aims to minimize the extent of permanent paralysis that the patient may experience throughout their life. Randomized controlled trials have been conducted to evaluate the efficacy of steroid treatments in acute spinal cord injury. Specifically, methylprednisolone sodium succinate has been shown to improve neurological outcomes when administered within eight hours of the injury. The recommended dosing regimen involves an initial bolus of 30 mg/kg given over 15 minutes, followed by a maintenance infusion of 5.4 mg/kg per hour for 23 hours. This protocol was first validated in a North American trial and subsequently replicated in a Japanese study, though not in a French trial. However, data from all three trials were combined in a meta-analysis, which confirmed significant motor function recovery when methylprednisolone therapy was initiated within the eight-hour window. A more recent study suggests that extending the maintenance infusion to 48 hours, rather than 23 hours, provides additional improvements in motor and functional recovery. This extended regimen appears particularly beneficial when treatment cannot begin until three to eight hours after the injury. Furthermore, methylprednisolone therapy has also demonstrated efficacy in treating whiplash injuries and has shown benefits in recovery following surgery for lumbar disc disease when a modified regimen is used. The largest trials investigating methylprednisolone therapy reported a low risk of bias. Importantly, there was no significant evidence of increased complications or mortality associated with either the 23-hour or 48-hour treatment protocols. In conclusion, high-dose methylprednisolone remains the only pharmacologic therapy with proven efficacy in phase three randomized trials for acute spinal cord injury, provided it is administered within eight hours of the injury. Extending the maintenance dose to 48 hours may offer additional benefits if treatment initiation is delayed. However, there is a critical need for further randomized trials to explore additional pharmacologic therapies for this condition.
